To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the relationship between sensory sensitivities and later social difficulties is complex and likely to vary across individuals, 2) sensory sensitivities may be a risk factor for social difficulties in ASC, 3) sensory sensitivities are not a primary feature of ASC, but rather a risk factor for ASC that interacts with other risk factors, such as social deficits, 4) sensory sensitivities in ASC may reflect an early developing feature of the condition and may be present in infancy, and 5
the social and sensory aspects of ASC are not independent, and that the social aspects of ASC are secondary to the sensory aspects.
1) Sensory and social features are both important in ASC, 2) Sensory difficulties may be a primary feature, and 3) Sensory and motivational features are not primary features of ASC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how sensory and nonsocial features relate to social features of ASC.
the sensory and social features of ASC, and how they can be integrated.
the relationship between sensory, social, and other aspects of ASC, and the mechanisms by which they are related to one another.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between sensory features and social difficulties in ASC is complex.
the evidence presented in this special issue does not provide support for a single, unified theory of ASC, in which sensory and social difficulties can be explained under a common framework.
sensory and social features of ASC are not independent of each other, and that the sensory and social features are both present early in development and are related to each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sensory features of ASC are not just secondary to social difficulties, but are a primary component of this condition.
sensory features are important to consider in the assessment and diagnosis of autism.
sensory and social features of ASC may be integrated, and that sensory features are likely to be a primary feature of ASC, rather than a secondary feature that arises from a primary social deficit.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the face processing deficits in FXS are similar to those seen in ASC, but that they are not the same.
infants with FXS have a different face processing system than those with low autism risk, with a more immature pattern of brain activation and reduced attention to faces.
the mGluR model is not sufficient to account for all of the face processing deficits seen in FXS.
